strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK increase causes register spill and instruction explosion
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (256–2048) caused the compiler to select a configuration that ballooned registers per thread from 22 to 58, cutting theoretical occupancy from 100% to 50% and achieved occupancy from 53% to 42%. Simultaneously, executed instructions exploded from ~483K to ~3.6M (7.5x), indicating the autotuner selected a configuration that unrolled far more work per thread than beneficial. Despite improving scheduler eligibility (No Eligible dropped from 54% to 19%), the net effect was a 2.2x longer kernel duration because the instruction count increase and occupancy loss outweighed the latency-hiding benefit.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: fixed small tile, low register pressure
@triton.jit
def kernel(... XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):  # XBLOCK=128, 22 regs/thread
    xindex = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)
    xmask = tl.full([XBLOCK], True, tl.int1)  # no bounds check
    tmp0 = tl.load(ptr + xindex, None)
    # ... BN + residual + ReLU ...
    tl.store(ptr + xindex, result, None)
grid = (cdiv(N, 128),)  # 1568 CTAs, 0.74 waves/SM
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER (regressed): autotuned larger tile, high register pressure
@triton.autotune(configs=[Config({'XBLOCK': 2048}, num_warps=8), ...], key=['xnumel'])
@triton.jit
def kernel(... XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):  # selected XBLOCK=256, 58 regs/thread
    xindex = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)
    xmask = xindex < xnumel  # bounds check added
    tmp0 = tl.load(ptr + xindex, xmask)
    # ... BN + residual + ReLU ...
    tl.store(ptr + xindex, result, xmask)
grid = lambda meta: (cdiv(N, meta['XBLOCK']),)  # dynamic grid
applicable_when: Never apply this specific pattern when the baseline kernel already has low register pressure (<=24 regs/thread) and 100% theoretical occupancy — increasing XBLOCK via autotune risks the compiler selecting a config that causes register pressure to spike (>48 regs/thread), halving theoretical occupancy and multiplying instruction count.
do_not_apply_when: Do not add @triton.autotune with large XBLOCK configs to pointwise kernels where: (1) baseline registers/thread is already low (<30), (2) theoretical occupancy is already at 100%, and (3) the kernel body contains many intermediate temporaries (BN normalization has ~10+ tmps). The autotune overhead and compiler register allocation for large tiles will cause instruction explosion and occupancy collapse. Also avoid when the grid is already small (<2000 CTAs) and the kernel is short (<5us) — autotune calibration cost dominates.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: @triton.autotune with large XBLOCK forces the JIT compiler to allocate registers for all XBLOCK elements simultaneously. For kernels with many intermediate values (e.g., batch norm: ~10 temporaries), XBLOCK=2048 requires 2048*10 virtual registers, causing spilling. The winning autotune config (XBLOCK=256, 58 regs) still doubled register pressure vs baseline (XBLOCK=128, 22 regs). In CUDA, the equivalent anti-pattern is increasing thread-level loop unroll factor beyond register file capacity.

strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK increase causes register spill and 7x instruction explosion
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (256–2048) caused the compiler to select XBLOCK=256 with 58 registers/thread (up from 22), cutting theoretical occupancy from 100% to 50% and achieved occupancy from 53% to 41%. More critically, executed instructions exploded from 482K to 3.6M (7.4x), indicating the larger tile triggered significant register pressure and likely loop unrolling overhead that dwarfed any latency-hiding benefit. The waves/SM improved from 0.74 to 2.97 and scheduler idle cycles dropped from 54% to 17%, but the 7x instruction count increase dominated, causing a 2.1x slowdown in wall time.
slow_pseudocode:
# Before: fixed XBLOCK=128, 22 registers/thread, 100% theoretical occupancy
@triton.jit
def kernel(... XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK  # XBLOCK=128
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    xmask = tl.full([XBLOCK], True, tl.int1)  # no bounds check
    # 5 loads + BN math + residual add + ReLU + store

grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # 1568 blocks
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)
fast_pseudocode:
# After (REGRESSED): autotune selected XBLOCK=256, 58 registers/thread, 50% theoretical occupancy
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 2048}, num_warps=8),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 1024}, num_warps=8),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 512},  num_warps=8),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 256},  num_warps=4),  # selected
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128},  num_warps=4),
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(... XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel  # bounds check added
    # same math but 7.4x more instructions executed

grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)
kernel[grid](...)  # autotune picks worst config
applicable_when: Never apply this pattern when the kernel already has low register usage (≤24 registers/thread) and 100% theoretical occupancy — increasing XBLOCK will cause register pressure that destroys occupancy.
do_not_apply_when: Do not add @triton.autotune with large XBLOCK configs to kernels where: (1) registers/thread is already near the limit for full occupancy (Block Limit Registers is the binding constraint), (2) the kernel body is compute-heavy enough that larger tiles cause register spill, (3) the bottleneck is low waves/SM but the kernel is already register-efficient at the current block size. The instruction count explosion (7x here) is a strong signal that the autotune selected a config that triggered unrolling/spill overhead.
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune with large XBLOCK values causes the compiler to unroll loops and allocate more registers. When registers/thread jumps from 22 to 58, Block Limit Registers drops from 21 to 4 blocks/SM, halving theoretical occupancy. The xmask bounds-check change (from tl.full True to xindex < xnumel) also adds predication overhead across all loads/stores when XBLOCK does not evenly divide the problem size — though in this case all configs divided evenly, so this was not the cause.
